clue.text: Romeo joins musical theatre company in US city

blocks.note: Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
English National Opera, the London opera company

explanation.surface: An actor called Romeo signs up with a touring company playing an American city.
explanation.definitionFit: Reno is a city in Nevada, famous for gambling and quick divorces.

clue.text: European operating systems for trade fairs

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for European
two systems: Windows XP, and OS, the abbreviation for operating system

explanation.surface: Software from European firms showcased at industry exhibitions.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'systems' is read as two of them: XP, the Windows version, and the generic abbreviation OS.
explanation.definitionFit: An expo is a large exhibition, and trade fairs are commercial exhibitions of that kind.

clue.text: Smelly rubbish on road finally swept

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word beside it
rubbish, read as a verb or as junk, says the letters are a mess to be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
last letter of swept

explanation.surface: Stinking rubbish lying in the road has at last been cleared away.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, odorant means giving off a smell, a fancier word for smelly.

clue.text: Press one to change message back

indicators.note: changing the letters means putting them in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An automated phone menu: press one to alter the message you send in return.
explanation.definitionFit: A reply sent in return to a communication is a response.

clue.text: Yankee feeds crew unlimited whisky

indicators.note: without limits means the word loses its boundary letters at both ends
one thing feeding another goes into it

blocks.note: crew with its first and last letters removed
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An American hands out unlimited whisky to a ship's crew.
explanation.definitionFit: Rye is whisky distilled from rye grain, especially in North America.

clue.text: Flying squad eyes new suspect

indicators.note: suspect as an adjective means dodgy, not to be trusted as it stands, so the letters need rearranging

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Detectives from a police unit size up a fresh suspect.
explanation.walkthrough: The Flying Squad is a Metropolitan Police robbery unit; Cockney rhyming slang calls it the Sweeney, from Sweeney Todd.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweeney is London slang for the Flying Squad, made famous by the 1970s TV police drama.

clue.text: Alert, for a woman performing tango in lead roles

indicators.note: in places the single letter inside the longer word

blocks.note: a performer is on, on stage
the heroes are the leading parts in a story
tango is T in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A dancer is on her toes, alert while performing the tango in a starring role.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is 'on his toes' or 'on her toes'; 'for a woman' tells you which pronoun to use.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on one's toes is an idiom for being ready and watchful.

clue.text: Dandy waves at sea

blocks.note: first meaning: a fashionable, smartly dressed man
second meaning: the long rolling movement of the open ocean

explanation.surface: A well-dressed man waves from a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waves' reads as a verb, the dandy waving; it is the noun, the rolling sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A swell is old slang for a stylish gent, and also the heave of the ocean.

clue.text: Male band led by American conducting

blocks.note: abbreviation for American, as in US
the male pronoun
a ring is a circular band

explanation.surface: An all-male group fronted by an American, with the leader conducting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'led by' places the American piece in front of the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Ushering someone means guiding or escorting them, the sense of conducting a visitor somewhere.

clue.text: Grudging acceptance of Cockney male's cheery attitude

blocks.note: his with the h dropped, as a Cockney would say it
up as in upbeat, in good spirits
an attitude is a bodily posture, a pose

explanation.surface: A Londoner's sunny outlook is accepted only reluctantly.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney speech drops the h, so his becomes 'is. 'Attitude' here is the posture sense, as in striking an attitude.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'I suppose' is how one concedes a point without enthusiasm.

clue.text: Similar sounds in London's city gardens

blocks.note: EC is the postcode district of the City of London
to garden is to hoe; read as a verb

explanation.surface: Sounds bounce around the gardens of the City of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gardens' looks like a noun but is the verb: one who gardens hoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Echoes are reflected repetitions of a sound, so similar sounds heard again.

clue.text: Entertaining lady on stage is happy leaving the wings

indicators.note: with the wings cut away only the inner run of letters is left

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words once their ends are trimmed

explanation.surface: A performer is happy to step out from the theatre wings onto the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wings' suggests the sides of a theatre stage; here it means the outer letters of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A geisha is a Japanese hostess trained to entertain guests with music, dance and conversation.

clue.text: Supply the bread for Spooner's foul-smelling dish

indicators.note: Spooner's tells us to swap the opening sounds of two words, as the reverend did

blocks.note: rank means foul-smelling and a bowl is a dish; swap their first sounds

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to provide bread to go with a nasty-smelling meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' is slang for money, not the loaf the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To bankroll a venture is to finance it, and bread is slang for money.

clue.text: Posh jeweller's opening in Brighton, with a great deal

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: first letter of Brighton
oodles means lots

explanation.surface: An upmarket jeweller opens a Brighton branch at a bargain.
explanation.walkthrough: Boodles is a British luxury jewellery firm; 'a great deal' looks like a bargain but means a lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Boodles is the name of an upmarket British jewellery retailer, so its shop is the posh jeweller's.

clue.text: Record deduction, taking 50% off

indicators.note: removing fifty percent leaves just half of the word

blocks.note: a discount is a deduction from the price

explanation.surface: A record reduction in price: half off everything.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half of the eight-letter word is dropped. 'Record deduction' reads as an all-time high, but 'Record' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A disc is a gramophone record or other recording medium.

clue.text: Intriguing links college graduate found between taste and sex

indicators.note: found between places the middle pieces inside the two others

blocks.note: to lick is to taste
it is a familiar euphemism for sex
standard abbreviation for college
a Bachelor of Arts

explanation.surface: A college graduate is found caught up in eye-catching links to food and sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' is a long-standing euphemism for sex. 'links' sounds like connections between the things named, but it is the definition: web links.
explanation.definitionFit: Clickbait is online content with teasing headlines designed to tempt people into following the link.

clue.text: Timber also something purchased, pro heard

indicators.note: heard means what follows is going by sound, not spelling

blocks.note: also is too, something purchased is a buy, pro is for

explanation.surface: A tradesperson hears about buying timber as well.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-by-four is a standard length of sawn timber, two inches by four in section.

clue.text: Enjoyed trustworthy but not competent cast

indicators.note: but not means take away the word that follows

blocks.note: trustworthy means dependable
competent means capable
to cast is to throw off, as a snake sheds skin

explanation.surface: A reviewer liked a reliable but not very competent acting cast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' reads as actors; it is the verb meaning throw off.
explanation.definitionFit: To relish something is to take great pleasure in it, so relished is a synonym of enjoyed.

clue.text: One cuts decorations down, being deliberately unproductive

indicators.note: cutting into something means going inside it

blocks.note: gongs is British slang for medals
the Roman numeral for one
feeling down is feeling low

explanation.surface: A worker is slow taking down the decorations, deliberately dawdling.
explanation.walkthrough: Gongs are British slang for medals or honours.
explanation.definitionFit: A go-slow is industrial action where workers slow down on purpose, so going slow is a protest of low output.

clue.text: Scrambled egg, or ei for a Hanoverian

indicators.note: scrambled things are mixed up out of their original order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Scrambled egg, or the German word for egg, served to a royal.
explanation.walkthrough: Ei is German for egg, a nod to the German-born king. George I was the first Hanoverian monarch of Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: George I was the first British king from the House of Hanover, so he is a Hanoverian.

clue.text: Lecturer's correcting text

indicators.note: a lecturer speaks, so what follows is taken by its spoken sound

blocks.note: righting a wrong is correcting it

explanation.surface: A lecturer marks and corrects an essay.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing is written text, the words set down on a page.

clue.text: Consequently see music one performs?

blocks.note: so means therefore
lo is an old word for look or see

explanation.surface: So, look at the music someone plays.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the wordplay on 'one': a piece performed by one person.
explanation.definitionFit: A solo is a piece of music played or sung by a single performer.

clue.text: Game ends in supposed deadlock - immediately son beats me

indicators.note: the ends of words are their last letters

blocks.note: Go is a Japanese board game
last letters of the two words
now means at once
standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A game ends in what looks like stalemate, and then the son suddenly beats his parent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beats me' is the colloquial 'I have no idea', not a defeat.
explanation.definitionFit: Both 'God knows' and 'beats me' are idioms for admitting one has no idea.

clue.text: Lyric connected with theatre

blocks.note: an ode is a lyric poem
on as in a book on birds, meaning about or connected with

explanation.surface: Something to do with the Lyric, a London theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lyric is a real London theatre, which hides that 'Lyric' is the poem here.
explanation.definitionFit: Odeon is a chain of cinemas, and also the ancient Greek word for a building for music.

clue.text: Funny poem is set as task

indicators.note: funny in the sense of odd or peculiar, so the letters come out strangely ordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A teacher sets a comic poem as homework.
explanation.definitionFit: To impose is to lay a duty or burden on someone, setting it for them.

clue.text: Unmetered parking went up

blocks.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
rose is the past tense of rise

explanation.surface: Parking charges have gone up now the meters are gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unmetered' suggests parking meters; it means without poetic metre.
explanation.definitionFit: Prose is ordinary writing without verse rhythm, the opposite of poetry with a set metre.

clue.text: What parts chimed in show again?

indicators.note: something parting another splits it open and sits within

blocks.note: bells chimed, or rang
eh? is a request to repeat, like what?

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about which sections of a show the bells rang in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What' looks like the start of a question; it is the exclamation eh.
explanation.definitionFit: Galleries rehang pictures when they put them on display again in a fresh arrangement.

clue.text: Bruce's number one Hey! Baby let emotions show

indicators.note: number one is the first in line, so the opening letter

blocks.note: first letter of Bruce
oi! is a shout to get attention
baby as a term of endearment

explanation.surface: Springsteen's chart-topping song 'Hey! Baby' gets everyone emotional.
explanation.walkthrough: Bruce suggests Springsteen; it only supplies a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To boil over is to lose control of one's feelings, as a pan spills when too hot.

clue.text: Head on board, US sailor coming over

indicators.note: coming over suggests turning over, so the word is read the other way

blocks.note: gob is American slang for a seaman

explanation.surface: A US sailor comes aboard and heads for the ship.
explanation.walkthrough: On a ship the toilet is the head; bog is British slang for toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A bog is a toilet in British slang, and the head is the toilet aboard ship.

clue.text: A night at sea east of New York, just one example

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place

blocks.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation for New York
night with its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: A night out sailing off the coast of New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'east of' puts the jumbled word after NY, as east is to the right on a map.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything means whatever one item you like, any single example at all.

clue.text: Grand old estate left by sugar magnate is sold

indicators.note: left by means abandoned, so the named letters are departed from the word

blocks.note: G for grand, a thousand
standard abbreviation for old
taken as written
Henry Tate, of the Tate & Lyle sugar company

explanation.surface: A grand old country estate abandoned by a sugar baron is put on the market.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Tate founded the sugar firm that became Tate & Lyle, and the Tate gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: At an auction, an item that goes is sold, as in 'going, going, gone'.
